pulls.title: refactor: keep duration calculations typed
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Several fixed-duration calculations use raw integer time counts, leaving their units implicit and allowing unrelated integer values to be mixed.

**Fix:** Use `std::chrono` types through calculations where the surrounding APIs already support them, including GUI formatting, peer bans, scheduler forwarding, block timestamps, and target-spacing arithmetic.
Where carrying chrono through an integer interface would broaden the change or make the result harder to read, this PR leaves the expression unchanged or keeps the conversion simply `duration / 1s`.
The remaining integer interfaces receive the same values, and characterization tests pin the PoW timing and inclusive assumevalid threshold.

pulls.title: p2p: prevent BIP35 requesters from bypassing inbound tx-relay capacity
pulls.body:
**Problem:** When a node offers `NODE_BLOOM`, an inbound peer can advertise `fRelay=false` and request BIP35 mempool inventory while remaining outside the inbound transaction-relay capacity introduced in [#28463](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28463).

**Fix:** Ignore `mempool` requests while the peer has transaction relay disabled, unless the connection has the `mempool` permission.
A BIP37 `filterload` message enables transaction relay and applies the existing capacity limit, preserving bitcoinj's [SPV `filterload`-then-`mempool` sequence](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35874#issuecomment-5278621654).
Targeted `getdata` requests remain unchanged.

pulls.title: script: clarify implicit signature-cache input requirements
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Signature-cache hashing relies on input requirements that are implicit at its public entry methods.
Inspired by the Elements rangeproof-cache vulnerability behind the recent [Liquid incident](https://blog.blockstream.com/liquid-network-security-incident-assessment) and the [subsequent cache-key fix](https://github.com/ElementsProject/elements/pull/1600), this change clarifies an easy-to-misread hashing pattern: `Write(data, size)` hashes the data bytes without encoding the size.
Bitcoin Core's cache keys already include the signature hash, public key, and signature in separate ECDSA and Schnorr domains.
Bitcoin Core's signature-cache encoding is unambiguous for inputs accepted by its current script checker: a valid ECDSA public key's prefix determines its length, while a Schnorr public key is always 32 bytes, leaving the signature as the remaining suffix.

**Fix:** Use native `HashWriter` serialization in the typed `ComputeEntry*` methods so ECDSA public keys and signature vectors include their CompactSize lengths.
Schnorr retains its fixed-size public-key encoding and raw signature span.
Return the digest by value from the public `ComputeEntry*` methods so callers explicitly initialize the cache entry, where the previous chained `Finalize(entry.begin())` obscured the output assignment.
Keep the prepared salt prefixes private and const, and copy them locally for each entry.
Add a nonce-taking constructor so tests can reproduce the encoding deterministically.
The process-local cache-entry bytes change, while script validity rules are unchanged.

pulls.title: net: reject oversized outbound messages
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Outbound transports encode message types in a fixed 12-byte field, but `CConnman` did not ensure internal callers respected this limit before queuing messages.
An oversized type aborts V1 encoding. V2 sends it under a truncated type with its payload intact, or writes past its encoding buffer when the payload is shorter than the excess type bytes.
The send path also did not enforce the 4 MB payload limit.

**Fix:** Treat oversized types and payloads as failed assumptions in `CConnman::PushMessage()` before they enter the send queue.

pulls.title: wallet: Fix ScanForWalletTransactions missing tx when look-ahead pool expands mid-block
pulls.body:
When `ScanForWalletTransactions` processes a block containing both a transaction to a key just outside the look-ahead pool and a pool-expanding transaction that triggers `TopUp`, and the former appears first in vtx order, the wallet misses the earlier transaction — leaving the balance wrong with no indication a second scan is needed. The fix retries any transaction that doesn't match on a full pass, dropping it once it does, until a pass resolves nothing new — so a transaction can be recognized once something else in the block makes it relevant, regardless of why. The first commit demonstrates the incorrect behaviour; the second contains the fix; the third adds a benchmark guarding the fix's performance on a large, mostly-foreign block with an embedded multi-level cascade.
Bug details...
`ScanForWalletTransactions` iterates over a block's transactions in the order the miner placed them (vtx order). A descriptor wallet maintains a look-ahead pool of pre-derived keys so it can recognise incoming payments. When a payment arrives at a key near the pool boundary, `MarkUnusedAddresses` → `TopUp` extends the pool. If within a single block: - **Tx_lookahead** pays to key index `N` (just outside the current pool `[0, N-1]`), AND - **Tx_expand** pays to key index `N-1` (last in pool — triggers TopUp, extending pool to `[0, 2N-1]`) and Tx_lookahead appears at an earlier vtx position than Tx_expand, the scan misses Tx_lookahead: 1. Tx_lookahead processed: pool = `[0, N-1]` → `IsMine` returns false → missed 2. Tx_expand processed: key `N-1` found → TopUp fires → pool = `[0, 2N-1]` `FastWalletRescanFilter::UpdateIfNeeded()` fires only at the **start of the next block** iteration — there is no mechanism to re-examine Tx_lookahead within the same scan pass. The transaction is not permanently lost — because Tx_expand extended the pool as a side effect, a second explicit `rescanblockchain` call recovers Tx_lookahead. But the wallet shows a wrong balance with no indication a second scan is needed. This bug does not affect live `blockConnected` when both transactions pass through the mempool first: `transactionAddedToMempool(Tx_expand)` pre-extends the pool before the block arrives, so vtx ordering does not matter. It only manifests in `ScanForWalletTransactions` (rescan paths) for descriptor wallets.
Affected callers...
**Callers affected** (all use `ScanForWalletTransactions`): - `rescanblockchain` - `importdescriptors` (via `RescanFromTime`) - `restorewallet` and wallet migration watchonly/solvable wallets (via `AttachChain`)
Fix details and performance...
**Fix:** during the per-block vtx loop, keep a list of still-unmatched vtx positions. Retry it each pass, dropping positions once `SyncTransaction()` returns `true` for them, until a full pass resolves nothing new. A transaction becomes resolvable once something else earlier in the same block changes its relevance — either a pool expansion (`TopUp` from `MarkUnusedAddresses`) now covering a key it pays, or a previously-unknown parent transaction becoming known so a spend of it is recognized. The unmatched set never grows, so this terminates without a safety cap. This also covers two cases a shrinking-prefix rescan (an earlier version of this fix) did not: a prefix-recovered receive that triggers a second pool expansion past where the prefix had already shrunk to (see Part 5), and a same-block spend of a look-ahead receive only recognized later in the same pass via a parent-tx lookup rather than a pool expansion (see Part 6, molnard's finding — see Notes below). **Performance:** the retry loop costs at most one extra pass for any block containing a wallet-relevant transaction during a rescan, in typical shapes. The worst case is a large, mostly-foreign block with a multi-level cascade embedded in it. `bench_bitcoin -filter=RescanCascadeInLargeBlock` guards that scenario against regression.
Test coverage...
**Regression test:** `test/functional/wallet_rescan_intrablock_ordering.py` - Part 1: loadwallet rescan — Tx_lookahead found after fix. - Part 2: importdescriptors full rescan from genesis — Tx_lookahead found after fix. - Part 3: second rescanblockchain recovers Tx_lookahead (pre-fix behaviour, kept as sanity check). - Part 4: two-level cascade — two successive TopUp events fire in one block, both lookahead txs found, validating the bounded multi-pass loop. - Part 5: a prefix-recovered receive triggers a second TopUp past where a shrinking-prefix rescan would have already stopped. - Part 6: a same-block spend of a look-ahead receive only recognized later in the same pass (molnard's finding).
Manual reproduction (regtest) ```bash bitcoind -regtest -keypool=5 -fallbackfee=0.0001 -daemon bitcoin-cli -regtest -named createwallet wallet_name=funding bitcoin-cli -regtest generatetoaddress 102 $(bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=funding getnewaddress) bitcoin-cli -regtest -named createwallet wallet_name=test RECV_DESC=$(bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=test listdescriptors \ | jq -r '[.descriptors[] | select(.internal==false and .range!=null)][0].desc') END_RANGE=$(bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=test listdescriptors \ | jq '[.descriptors[] | select(.internal==false and .range!=null)][0].range[1]') ADDR_EXPAND=$(bitcoin-cli -regtest deriveaddresses "$RECV_DESC" "[$END_RANGE,$END_RANGE]" | jq -r '.[0]') ADDR_LOOKAHEAD=$(bitcoin-cli -regtest deriveaddresses "$RECV_DESC" "[$((END_RANGE+1)),$((END_RANGE+1))]" | jq -r '.[0]') bitcoin-cli -regtest unloadwallet test TXID1=$(bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=funding sendtoaddress "$ADDR_LOOKAHEAD" 0.001) TXID2=$(bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=funding sendtoaddress "$ADDR_EXPAND" 0.001) bitcoin-cli -regtest generateblock "raw(51)" "[\"$TXID1\",\"$TXID2\"]" # First scan — TXID1 missing, wrong balance bitcoin-cli -regtest loadwallet test bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=test listtransactions # Second scan — TXID1 recovered bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=test rescanblockchain bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=test listtransactions # With the fix (this PR's tip), both transactions are found on the first scan. bitcoin-cli -regtest loadwallet test bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=test listtransactions ```
_**Notes**_: * Originally noted by furszy in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31629#issuecomment-2657775368; his "case 2" describes a related but harder inter-block variant: new blocks arriving via `blockConnected` during an active rescan with a not-yet-expanded pool. That problem remains a potential follow-up. This PR fixes the simpler intra-block sub-case where the miss happens entirely within a single block's vtx loop, with no concurrent block arrivals required. * Perhaps the issue is related to the symptom was previously reported in #19808 but could not be reproduced at the time and was closed without a fix. * molnard [found](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35901#pullrequestreview-5041935034) a related gap the shrinking-prefix rescan didn't close: if a parent tx pays a look-ahead key and a later tx in the same block spends that parent's output, and the spend sits at or after the block's last pool expansion, the prefix rescan recovers the parent but never revisits the spend. jeanpablojp separately found a second gap in the same shrinking-prefix approach — a prefix-recovered receive that triggers a further pool expansion past where the prefix had already shrunk to (Part 5) — and proposed and benchmarked the fix now in this PR: retry based on each tx's `SyncTransaction()` result until a full pass causes no change, rather than tracking a shrinking prefix. Both gaps are now fixed in this PR (Parts 5 and 6).

pulls.title: First steps towards a stateless, side-effect free validation library
pulls.body:
This implements the following actions from #35904:

1. **Expose the validation interface**

   Make the existing `CheckBlockHeader`, `ContextualCheckBlockHeader`, and `ContextualCheckBlock` functions part of the public validation interface by declaring them in `validation.h`.

2. **Interface Segregation: Remove dependency on `ChainstateManager`**

   `ContextualCheck*` functions need a  `ChainstateManager` only to access the
  consensus parameters. Pass `Consensus::Params` instead and access them at the call site.

3. **Make environmental dependencies explicit**

pulls.title: descriptor: Represent multipath descriptors in a single Descriptor object
pulls.body:
Currently, multipath descriptor strings treat the multipath specifiers as syntactic sugar. Once we finish parsing such a string, the multipath elements are lost as the result is the multiple distinct descriptors that the multipath is a shorthand for. This means that we are unable to return the multipath string for such descriptors.

This PR allows descriptors to actually be multipath where the multipath specifiers are represented inside of the paths of `BIP32PubkeyProvider`s. This allows for the multipath string to be produced.

In order to achieve this, a lot of derivation path parsing is refactored. `KeyPath` is promoted to being its own class (which subclasses `std::vector`), while the individual derivation indexes become a `KeyPathElement` object so that the multipath elements can be represented. Furthermore, hardened derivation characters are now being stored within `KeyPathElement`s so each element knows what the original hardened character was. This also cleans up a little bit of the descriptor implementation as we no longer have to carry around `bool apostrophe` in a bunch of places.

Lastly, `Parse` now returns a single `Descriptor` object, rather than a vector of them. If the descriptor is a multipath descriptor, the expansion can be retrieved using `GetMultipathExpansion()`. The wallet uses this and still must not store multipath descriptors.

pulls.title: descriptor: Reconstruct a multipath descriptor from its expansion
pulls.body:
#36442 allows multipath descriptors to be represented in a single `Descriptor` object. `GetMultipathExpansion` returns the multiple descriptors represented by a multipath descriptor. This expansion is reversible - given the expansion in the order of the multipath elements, it is possible to determine what the original multipath descriptor was. This PR adds `ReconstructMultipath` to produce a new `Descriptor` representing the multipath descriptor that produced the expansion.

Depends on #36442

pulls.title: wallet: Store information about created and imported multipath descriptors
pulls.body:
The wallet does not store any information about multipath descriptors. When a multipath descriptor is imported, it is first expanded, then the expansion descriptors are imported into the wallet.

This PR adds a field to `WalletDescriptor` which stores the IDs of the ScriptPubKeyMans of the descriptors that are part of the expansion, in the order that they are expanded. This allows us to use `ReconstructMultipath` to produce the multipath descriptor when necessary.

This is useful for working with hardware wallets that require policy registration, particularly those that require resending the descriptor that was registered.

`listdescriptors` is updated to include a `multipath_descriptor` field which contains the multipath descriptor for each individual descriptor if it originally came from a multipath descriptor.

Lastly, the automatically generated descriptors are now produced and stored as multipath descriptors, so `listdescriptors` will provide a `multipath_descriptor` for everything that the wallet automatically generates.

Note that the IDs stored in the wallet are ScriptPubKeyMan IDs, which we cannot compute from a descriptor as we assume to be opaque blobs since #35445.

Alternative to #36133, depends on #36442 and #36443

pulls.title: fuzz: improve ipc fuzz coverage
pulls.body:
This PR follows up on #35118 and continues the IPC fuzzing work proposed in #23015.

The initial ipc fuzz target exercised normal calls through a libmultiprocess client and server. This PR extends the target with

 - Server side assertions that verify arguments arrive unchanged (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35118#issuecomment-4452992198 and https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35118#pullrequestreview-4539477599)
 - A callback call that exercises ipc communication in both directions.
 - Raw capnp requests containing arbitrary transaction and `UniValue` payloads, which are deserialized by a normal libmultiprocess server.
  - Raw capnp responses containing arbitrary transaction and `UniValue` payloads, which are deserialized by a normal libmultiprocess client.

The raw request and response cases allow the fuzz target to exercise deserialization with data that was not first produced by libmultiprocess serialization.

The ipc setup and callback handling closely follow the existing [`libmultiprocess` tests](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/src/ipc/libmultiprocess/test/mp/test/test.cpp), particularly their use of `EventLoop`, `ProxyClient`, `ProxyServer`, two-way pipes, and `initThreadMap`. 

The transaction and UniValue payload cases exercise the serialization hooks defined in [`common-types.h`](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/src/ipc/capnp/common-types.h). 

These files may provide useful background when reviewing the changes.

Generated [coverage report](https://enirox001.github.io/coverage/ipc/) after fuzzing the IPC target for a while using the qa-assets corpus.

pulls.title: descriptor: Expose key expression parsing
pulls.body:
This PR exposes a utility function to parse and validate a standalone descriptor key expression. 
This is particularly useful in GUI multisig setup flows where the UI accepts a pasted key expression. The GUI can use this parser to validate input, inspect the parsed key,  and apply setup-specific policy i.e. reject private keys, uncompressed keys etc. (Multisig Wizard tracking issue: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/35645)

`PubkeyProvider` is the existing internal representation of a parsed key expression. This PR exposes its interface in `descriptor.h` and adds a public `ParsePubkey()` overload that returns the providers produced by the existing parser.

Key changes
- public overload uses P2TR key rules, permitting compressed, x-only, extended, and MuSig key expressions while rejecting uncompressed keys.
- Add `GetOriginInfo()` for retrieving explicitly provided key origin information.

---
Also, while I'm here, I noticed that `musig` parser accepted trailing characters apart from `/`. 
- Add a fix & test to reject unexpected trailing characters after a `musig()` expression

pulls.title: net_processing: Ignore MSG_WITNESS_TX entries from INV messages
pulls.body:
When introducing wtxidrelay we added checks to skip attempts to announce txs with the wrong hash (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/18044#discussion_r403953004), but didn't similarly ignore `MSG_WITNESS_TX` entries in announcements, which have never been valid (see [BIP-144](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0144.mediawiki#relay)).

This PR corrects that oversight, skipping such announcements. It also moves the check to be after the disconnect code, so that attempting to announce txs on `fRelay=false` doesn't get treated as okay just because you're doing it wrong. As a result this allows deduping the `seen_tx_hashes` set.

pulls.title: net: reject oversized locators before allocating
pulls.body:
**Problem:** `getblocks` and `getheaders` enforce `MAX_LOCATOR_SZ` only after deserializing locator hashes.
A truncated locator advertising an oversized count makes generic vector deserialization fail before the disconnect check, leaving the peer connected.

**Fix:** Read the advertised count before allocating hashes and disconnect when it exceeds the existing limit.
Catch only the size-limit error so other deserialization failures remain non-disconnecting.
Complete oversized locators continue to disconnect without discouragement, and `p2p_invalid_locator.py` verifies that both messages accept 101 hashes and disconnect at 102.

pulls.title: net: allow selecting BIP152 high-bandwidth peers with `-addnode`
pulls.body:
Bitcoin Core automatically selects up to three BIP152 high-bandwidth peers after they deliver useful blocks. This works for ordinary connections, but it cannot use topology information known by the operator.

For example, an operator may run nodes in multiple locations or maintain a stable, low-latency peering link and want that connection to announce compact blocks immediately and consistently, including after reconnects, instead of waiting for automatic selection.

This PR adds an opt-in suffix:

```
-addnode=<host>[:port]=bip152-hb
```
A matching outbound peer receives the existing `SENDCMPCT(1)` request after the handshake. The policy is reapplied on reconnect and requires no new P2P protocol messages.

Configured peers are additional to the three automatically selected peers and are not included in automatic rotation. This intentionally allows explicit configuration to exceed BIP152’s current three-peer limit and may increase redundant bandwidth. If accepted, BIP152 can be updated separately.

The option is incompatible with `-blocksonly`. Untagged addnodes, inbound connections, and the addnode RPC retain their existing behavior; RPC support can be considered separately.

From the Boost.MultiIndex [docs](https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/latest/libs/multi_index/doc/tutorial/debug.html#invariant_check):

Define it in the two jobs that already define `BOOST_MULTI_INDEX_ENABLE_SAFE_MODE`. The "MSAN, fuzz" job also defines safe mode but is left unchanged, as invariant checking would push it past the 240-minute limit on the Warp runner.

pulls.title: wallet: harden the read-only BDB parser against crafted files
pulls.body:
The read-only BDB parser in migrate.cpp runs on any file passed to `migratewallet`
(RPC or GUI) or `bitcoin-wallet`. #34959 added checks for btree levels and overflow
lengths, which stop simple cycles, but a crafted file can still make the parser hang
or use a lot of memory:

- A btree page can be the child of more than one internal page. Its level still
  checks out, so it gets parsed again for every path that reaches it. On master an
  ~8 KB file built this way doesn't finish.
- An overflow page with no data doesn't count toward the length #34959 checks, so
  two such pages pointing at each other loop forever. Separately, any number of
  records can point at the same overflow chain, and each one reads and stores its
  own copy.
- All of a page's index entries can point at the same record, which then gets read
  and kept once per entry. A single 64 KB page can turn into ~500 MB this way. On
  master a 256 KB file took `migratewallet` from 54 MB to ~800 MB.

The first two are fixed by tracking visited pages (the approach from #34946): btree
pages in one set, and overflow pages in another that covers the whole tree. For the
third, a page is rejected once its records add up to more than the page size.

This shouldn't affect real wallets. In a valid btree every page has a single parent
and every overflow page belongs to a single record. Records on a page can't overlap
either, since the parser already rejects databases that allow duplicates.

Each fix comes with a test in db_tests.cpp that builds the bad file by hand, plus a
test that a page filled to the last byte still parses. `wallet_migration.py` passes
with v28.2.

The last commit adds two errors from #34959 to the `wallet_bdb_parser` fuzz target.
They were missing, so the target aborted on inputs that reach them. I ran into this
while feeding mutated copies of the test files through the target.

Supersedes #35992.

pulls.title: wallet: Handle or explicitly ignore `WalletBatch` write failures
pulls.body:
A common theme in the wallet is that many database write failures are ignored, when they should probably be handled, or at least documented that a failure is being ignored. This PR marks all database functions in `WalletBatch` as `[[nodiscard]]` so that a compiler will tell us if a return value is implicitly ignored. All of the calls to those functions are updated to either deal with failure, or explicitly ignore it with a rationale.

Based on #35752 which handles failures for the encryption functions.

pulls.title: validation: prefetch blocks while connecting
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Connecting a block already on disk requires reading and deserializing it.
Doing this on the validation thread stalls validation and slows reindexing and initial block download.

This is a follow-up to [#35295](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35295), which parallelized input prevout fetching during block connection.

**Fix:** Add a `Chainstate`-owned block fetcher that reads later blocks from disk while the current block is connected.
Start with synchronous 1-block read-ahead, then move reads to an eagerly started worker pool that persists across activations.
Keep caller-provided blocks on the direct path and refill a sliding read-ahead window.
During reorgs, start reading the first sibling while disconnecting the old tip.
Retry speculative failures synchronously when the block is needed.

`-blockfetchthreads=<n>` selects readers per chainstate, with a default of 2 and a cap of 16.
Setting it to 0 disables read-ahead. The window retains up to two blocks per reader, giving 4 by default.
Measurements favor 2 readers with a window of 4 or 8 blocks, so the default uses the smaller window.

**Credit:** The idea comes from [bitcoindev1337](https://bitcoin-irc.chaincode.com/bitcoin-core-dev/2026-08-11#1245429), who had already implemented a similar design and reported comparable results.

pulls.title: txindex: allow running in pruned mode
pulls.body:
After #35531, each txindex entry now points to the block hash containing the tx instead of the file location of the block. The block hash is then used to find the file position of the block to read the tx from. This allows us to determine the hash of the containing block even if the block is later pruned, and also determine the location of the block on disk if it is later downloaded again via `getblockfrompeer`.

This PR enables maintaining a txindex while pruned. If a txid lookup tries to read a tx from a pruned block, the hash of the missing block is surfaced to the caller.

If desired, a user may call `getblockfrompeer` using the returned hash to download the block, then try again successfully. The downloaded block will be added to the front of the block queue, so won't be pruned again for at least 288 blocks. Of course a larger prune setting is desired if lots of historical blocks will be read, and there are privacy issues if the user is looking up their own transactions. Ideally the blocks can be fetched from a trusted node or from random peers with decoy blocks fetched occasionally.

Resolves https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/10609, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/12651, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/16182, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/35240

pulls.title: rpc, descriptor: warn when multipath expansion clones single-path key expressions
pulls.body:
This PR:
  - deduplicate warnings pushed with `PushWarnings` in RPC calls
  - warn when single-path key expressions or tr() subscripts are cloned into every multipath expansion; surfaced by `importdescriptors` and by a new `warnings` field on `getdescriptorinfo` (which also exposes the existing miniscript `older()` warnings)

Cloning internal to musig() is not warned: both `musig(A,B)/<0;1>/*` and `musig(A/<1;2>,B)` derive a distinct aggregate key per branch, so nothing observable is reused.

closes #35985
